All four options are polymers of glucose, so the distinguishing feature is the **branching**.
The question states that glycogen has a C₁–C₄ backbone with C₁–C₆ branch points. Match that
against each:
**Amylose** — the unbranched fraction of starch, a straight α-1,4 chain only. No branching ✗
**Cellulose** — straight chain again, and β-1,4 rather than α. No branching ✗
**Glucose** — a monosaccharide, not a polymer at all ✗
**Amylopectin** — the branched fraction of starch: α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branch points ✓
That is exactly the pattern described, so glycogen resembles amylopectin.
Glycogen is in fact the more heavily branched of the two, with a branch roughly every 10
units against every 25 in amylopectin. That is why it is called 'animal starch' — the many
chain ends let enzymes release glucose quickly when it is needed.
∴ amylopectin.

The weight must be reported to **three** significant figures, so take the more precise reading
and round it.
The two results are 3.929 g (four significant figures) and 4.0 g (two).
Rounding 3.929 to three significant figures: the digits kept are 3, 9 and 2, and the first
digit dropped is 9.
Since 9 is greater than 5, round the last retained digit up:
3.929 ⇒ **3.93**
Check the alternatives: 3.90 would mean rounding down, which the trailing 9 forbids; 4.00
wrongly carries the rounding through two places; and 3.92 is simple truncation rather than
rounding.
The 4.0 g reading is consistent with this but is too coarse to decide the third figure, which
is why the finer balance governs.
∴ 3.93 g.

A **secondary** alcohol has its –OH on a carbon bonded to exactly **two** other carbons.
Take each structure.
(i) CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ — the carbinol carbon holds an ethyl, a methyl and one H. Two carbons
attached ⇒ **secondary** ✓
(ii) (C₂H₅)₃COH — the carbinol carbon holds three ethyl groups. Three carbons ⇒ tertiary ✗
(iii) C₆H₅OH — the –OH is attached directly to an **aromatic ring** carbon. That makes it a
phenol, not an alcohol at all ✗
(iv) C₆H₅CH(OH)CH₃ — the carbinol carbon holds a phenyl, a methyl and one H. Two carbons
attached ⇒ **secondary** ✓
So (i) and (iv) qualify.
Note (iii) is the deliberate trap: the OH looks similar but an sp² ring carbon puts it in an
entirely different class, with quite different chemistry — phenols are acidic, alcohols are not.
∴ (i) and (iv).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|1|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
An **intensive** property does not depend on the amount of matter present — temperature,
pressure, density, refractive index, and any molar quantity.
An **extensive** property does — mass, volume, enthalpy, entropy, heat capacity.
The test: cut the system in half. Whatever stays the same is intensive; whatever halves is
extensive.
(a) Temperature and density — both unchanged by halving ✓ both intensive
(b) Pressure and molar volume — pressure is unchanged, and *molar* volume is per mole, so
also unchanged ✓ both intensive
(c) Molar heat capacity and density — again both per-unit quantities ✓ both intensive
(d) **Heat capacity and enthalpy** — halve the sample and both halve. Both are **extensive** ✗
Note how (c) and (d) differ by a single word: *molar* heat capacity is intensive, plain heat
capacity is not.
∴ heat capacity and enthalpy.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|1|Pradeep Chemistry:
A Grignard reagent adds its alkyl group to the carbonyl carbon; acid hydrolysis then puts an
H on the oxygen. The class of alcohol produced depends on the carbonyl used:
methanal ⇒ **primary** alcohol
any other aldehyde ⇒ secondary alcohol
ketone ⇒ tertiary alcohol
The target, 1-butanol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH), is **primary** with four carbons, so the carbonyl
must be formaldehyde and the Grignard must supply three carbons.
(a) HCHO + n-C₃H₇MgBr ⇒ CH₃CH₂CH₂–CH₂OH ✓ four carbons, primary ✓
Check the others:
(b) Ethanal + ethylMgBr ⇒ butan-2-**ol**, secondary, wrong position.
(c) Propanone + methylMgBr ⇒ 2-methylpropan-2-ol, tertiary.
(d) An ester with one equivalent of Grignard gives a ketone and then a tertiary alcohol, not
a primary one.
∴ formaldehyde + n-propylmagnesium bromide.

The structure is a cyclopentane ring carrying a –CHO group.
The rule for naming an aldehyde attached to a **ring** is that the ring cannot be the parent
chain, because the –CHO carbon lies outside it. Instead the ring is named as the substituent
and the suffix **carbaldehyde** is used for the –CHO:
ring name + carbaldehyde ⇒ **cyclopentanecarbaldehyde** ✓
Now the others:
(c) 'Cyclopentanal' would imply the carbonyl carbon is C-1 **of the ring**, which it is not.
(a) 'Cyclopentane aldehyde' is not an accepted IUPAC construction.
(d) 'Cyclopentyl methanal' treats the CHO as methanal with a substituent — understandable,
but not the preferred name.
The same convention gives benzaldehyde its systematic name, benzenecarbaldehyde.
∴ cyclopentanecarbaldehyde.

This is a hypothetical question: suppose the stable configuration were **6** outer electrons
instead of 8.
Fluorine has 7 valence electrons (2s² 2p⁵).
Under the real octet rule it **gains** one electron to reach 8, giving F⁻.
Under the new rule it must reach 6, so it has one electron **too many** and must **lose** one:
F ⇒ F⁺ + e⁻
Removing one electron from 7 leaves 6 ✓
Losing an electron gives a **positive** ion, so the stable fluoride ion would be **F⁺**.
Options (c) F²⁺ and (d) F³⁺ would leave 5 and 4 electrons, overshooting the target of 6, and
(a) F⁻ is the answer under the actual octet rule, which is the trap.
The principle is the general one: an atom gains or loses whichever is the smaller number of
electrons to reach the stable count.
∴ F⁺.
